newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemalan army may end shutdown of oil refinery.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan army may end shutdown of oil refinery.

text.p: The army was poised on Monday to forcibly remove some 300 former paramilitary patrolmen who for five days have occupied an oil refinery in northern Guatemala, demanding pay for wartime service, officials said.

Production at Guatemala's only oil refinery has been halted since Thursday, when the former Civil Self-Defense Patrols occupied the Basic Resources International Ltd. plant in La Libertad in the northern department of Peten.
"We are waiting for an order from a judge. Security forces are there -- not only the civilian police but also the military -- ready to act," Vice President Luis Flores Asturias told reporters.

The Civil Self-Defense Patrols in the 1980s were a key component of Guatemala's counterinsurgency campaign against leftist guerrilas in a 36-year civil war that ended with the signing of a peace treaty last December.
The patrols were used to spy on suspected guerrilla sympathizers in rural towns and also came under intense criticism from human rights groups.

But now former patrol members are demanding pay for their role in helping the army. Their old foes, the guerrillas, have received government and international funds for resettlement programs under the terms of the peace accord.
"The government position is that the possibility of economic indeminization for them is totally exhausted," Raquel Zelaya, presidential secretary for peace, told reporters.
Basic produces 23,000 barrels of crude oil a day from 14 wells in Guatemala.
This is the third time this year the same group of disgruntled ex-patrolmen has occupied the La Libertad refinery. There are no hostages.

Though participation in the civil patrols was supposedly voluntary, in practice in many rural areas all men over 16 years old were forced to join up or risk being tagged as communist sympathizers. At their height in the mid 1980s an estimated 900,000 Guatemalan men belonged to patrols.
The government officially disbanded the patrols last year under the terms of the peace accord.
